identity.title: Adaptive Surrogate Gradients for Sequential Reinforcement Learning in Spiking Neural Networks

problem.claim: Train spiking neural networks for complex sequential reinforcement-learning control tasks.

gap.claim: Non-differentiable spikes make surrogate-gradient optimization properties unclear, while limited early-training sequence lengths can prevent SNNs from bridging their warm-up period.

contributions.claim: Systematic analysis of surrogate-gradient slope settings and their effects on gradient magnitude and alignment.
A training approach using a privileged guiding policy to bootstrap learning while retaining online interactions with the spiking policy.
Combining the approach with adaptive slope scheduling for real-world drone position control outperformed the cited prior techniques.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe the privileged-policy bootstrapping approach as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Authors report that shallower or scheduled slopes produced a ×2.1 improvement in both training and final deployed RL performance.
Authors report no clear fixed-versus-scheduled slope preference in supervised learning.
Authors report an average return of 400 points for real-world drone position control, versus at most −200 for Behavioral Cloning and TD3BC under the same conditions.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper frames neuromorphic SNN control as promising but identifies surrogate-gradient and sequential-RL warm-up challenges.
It analyzes slope settings, reporting a tradeoff between deeper-layer gradient magnitude and alignment with true gradients.
It reports no clear slope preference in supervised learning but a pronounced RL benefit from shallower or scheduled slopes.
It introduces privileged-policy bootstrapping and combines it with adaptive scheduling in a real-world drone task.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates slope behavior in supervised learning from its stronger effect in RL, then pairs slope scheduling with a task-specific bootstrapping method.

lessons.interpretation: Claiming regime-specific effects can make a technical argument more informative than presenting one universal hyperparameter rule.
lessons.application: When proposing an optimization technique, report whether its behavior differs across training regimes and connect that distinction to the method design.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the study evaluates only one regime or lacks evidence for cross-regime differences.

unknowns: The abstract does not define the slope parameterization or schedule, quantify gradient-alignment measures, or report uncertainty for the ×2.1 improvement.

Details of the privileged guiding policy, baselines, task conditions, and deployment protocol are unspecified; the reported return comparison is therefore not independently interpretable from the abstract alone.
